questions.prompt: What was the model intended to show?

stimulus.title: A model worth changing
stimulus.body: Sienna built a model street from cardboard and sand to show where rainwater might go. At first she concentrated on making the shops attractive. When she poured water at one end, a puddle formed behind a shop. Her display card described a drain, but the model had no channel leading to it. Sienna considered wiping away the puddle before anyone saw it. Instead, she removed the shop and cut a shallow channel towards a collection cup. For the next trial she used the same amount of water. The puddle became smaller, although some water still collected in the sand. At the exhibition, she displayed drawings of both trials and explained what she had changed. She also pointed out that a cardboard model could not show everything that happens in a real street.

How quickly cardboard grows
Where rainwater might go
Which street had the most people

questions.explanation: The opening sentence gives the model purpose.

questions.prompt: What do the volunteers promise?

stimulus.title: Repair day notice
stimulus.body: Community repair day will be held at the hall on Saturday from 10 am to 2 pm. Volunteers will help visitors explore safe repairs, but cannot promise that every object can be fixed. Bring one clean object and put any loose pieces in a bag. Do not bring appliances that must be plugged in or objects with leaking batteries. If you are unsure whether an object is suitable, ask at the welcome desk. No booking is needed: collect a number card when you arrive. A complicated repair may take longer than a simple one. Children must attend with an adult. At noon there will be a cloth-tear demonstration for everyone, including visitors whose objects cannot be repaired. Donations towards materials are welcome but optional. Please take your object home at the end; volunteers cannot keep unfinished repairs.

options.text: A replacement for every broken object
Electrical testing of plugged-in appliances
Storage of all unfinished objects
Help exploring safe repairs, rather than a repair for every object

questions.explanation: The notice offers help but explicitly gives no guarantee of repair.

questions.prompt: How did the paths on the two maps differ?

stimulus.title: The missing path
stimulus.body: Theo found two maps of the school garden. Both had the same year printed at the bottom. On one, a path crossed the middle; on the other, it followed the fence. The fence-path map also showed a new shed where the first map had an empty square. A photograph showed tools being carried into the shed on opening day in September. However, neither map gave a month, and the photograph did not show the path. Theo wrote that the fence-path map might be the later one. He kept both maps and noted the reasons for his uncertainty. Later, the caretaker remembered helping to pave a path beside the fence, but could not remember the month. Theo added this recollection as a separate note rather than changing the date printed on either map.

options.text: One crossed the middle and one followed the fence
Both followed exactly the same route
One showed a path inside the shed
Neither showed a path

questions.explanation: The opening comparison states the two routes.

questions.prompt: What problem did Maya's idea address?

stimulus.title: Two ideas for the bus stop
stimulus.body: Maya suggested painting a queue line at the school bus stop because late arrivals sometimes crowded around the bus door. She warned that a permanent line in the wrong place might make the crowding worse. Joel proposed a shelter to keep students dry. A shelter would require approval and money, so he suggested using the covered walkway during rain while planning continued. That temporary arrangement would only be safe if staff kept the passage clear for other people. The council agreed to try removable queue markers for two weeks, arrange staff supervision of the wet-weather walkway and obtain a cost estimate for a shelter. The school newsletter described the shelter as a proposal awaiting a decision, rather than an approved building project.

The price of bus tickets

questions.prompt: How long did each observation last?

stimulus.title: The pond notebook
stimulus.body: For six evenings, a class watched a pond from one marked point on the path. Each observation lasted fifteen minutes. Students counted visible ripples and recorded the weather, without touching plants or animals. On the first still evening they saw many clear ripples. On the third evening, wind made the surface difficult to read and the recorded count was lower. One student suggested that there must have been fewer animals. The teacher pointed out that the class had measured visible ripples, not animals: wind and falling leaves could also disturb the surface. The students added a column for observations they could not distinguish confidently and kept their viewing method the same. Their summary described six evenings of surface activity, rather than the entire pond population or a whole year. They included the limits as well as the numbers.

options.text: Six hours
One whole evening
Fifteen minutes
Three minutes

questions.explanation: The passage gives a fifteen-minute duration for each observation.
